frames.main_point: Aluminum tends to tolerate sudden high-G loads without cracking, while carbon fiber is much more rigid and therefore less forgiving under impact-type stresses.
frames.source_quote: Sudden high G-forces don't crack aluminum, carbon fiber on the other hand is very rigid.
frames.subject: aluminum flexibility vs carbon fiber rigidity

frames.label: Choose carbon fiber for a quadcopter frame if you are an experienced pilot who builds it right the first time and rar...
frames.main_point: Choose carbon fiber for a quadcopter frame if you are an experienced pilot who builds it right the first time and rarely crashes.
frames.source_quote: So if you are a professional R/C pilot, that build's it right the first time, and doesn't crash a lot, I would say Carbon fiber.
frames.subject: material choice for quadcopter frame (low crash rate)

frames.label: Select aluminum for a quadcopter frame if you expect frequent design changes, anticipate high stresses, or are a less...
frames.main_point: Select aluminum for a quadcopter frame if you expect frequent design changes, anticipate high stresses, or are a less experienced pilot who may crash more often.
frames.source_quote: If you make a lot of changes, are not a very good pilot, or think you are going to stress it a lot, I would say Aluminum.
frames.subject: material choice for quadcopter frame (frequent changes/high stress)

frames.source_quote: Aluminium is somewhat heavier and will transmit vibration (balance your motors and props) but is readily available cheaper and easier to work with.

semantic_edges.reasoning: Both prescribe opposite materials for overlapping scenarios. A recommends carbon fiber when crashes are rare (experienced pilot), while B recommends aluminum for smaller craft. For a small craft piloted by an experienced, low-crash pilot, A says carbon fiber and B says aluminum—directly conflicting guidance.
